[56] # Binary Search Tree and Inorder Traversal

A Binary Search Tree (BST) organizes hierarchical node data where every node contains a key, optional data, and pointers to left and right child nodes.

## The Inorder Traversal Invariant

Inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes by processing the left subtree, evaluating the current node, and subsequently traversing the right subtree.

Because all keys in the left child are strictly less than the root, and all keys in the right child are strictly greater, an inorder traversal of a binary search tree outputs elements in monotonically increasing sorted order. This makes BST traversal a natural mechanism for producing sorted output in O(n) linear time.

## Search and Balancing

Search starts at the root, moving to the left child if the target is smaller and to the right child if greater, terminating when found or reaching a null leaf.

Average time for lookup, insertion, and deletion is O(log n). If elements are inserted in ascending or descending sorted order without balancing, the tree degenerates into a linear chain with O(n) worst-case depth.

[18] # Graph Traversal: BFS and DFS

Graph traversal systematically visits nodes and edges in a network without cycling indefinitely.

## Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Breadth-First Search uses a queue to visit vertices layer by layer in order of graph distance from the origin. Starting at a root node, all immediate neighbors are visited before proceeding to distance two neighbors.

Because BFS explores outward evenly, it computes the exact shortest path in unweighted graphs. Time complexity is O(V + E) with O(V) space for the queue and visited state.

## Depth-First Search (DFS)

Depth-First Search explores deeply along connected branches before backtracking. It operates using recursion or an explicit stack.

DFS is suited for topological sorting, cycle detection, and finding strongly connected components. A cycle in a directed graph is detected if DFS encounters an edge pointing to an ancestor currently residing in the active recursion call stack.

[24] # Dijkstra Shortest Path Algorithm

Dijkstra algorithm determines the shortest path from a starting source node to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights.

## Relaxation with Priority Queue

The algorithm maintains a distance array initialized to zero for the source node and infinity for all others. A priority queue or min-heap tracks discovered vertices by minimum cumulative distance.

In each step, the vertex with the lowest tentative distance is extracted. For each outgoing edge to neighbor v, relaxation checks if the path through current node u provides a shorter distance than the previously recorded distance to v. If so, distance to v is updated and the pair is pushed to the min-heap.

## Runtime Complexity and Constraints

Using a standard binary min-heap, Dijkstra runs in O((V + E) log V) time. The algorithm is greedy and assumes that once a vertex distance is finalized, no future path can reduce it.

Because negative weights can violate this monotonic non-decreasing path distance property, Dijkstra fails on graphs with negative edges. In such scenarios, the Bellman-Ford algorithm must be used instead.

[53] # AVL Trees and Balancing Rotations

An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree that maintains logarithmic lookup depth under insertions and deletions.

## Height Balance Factor

The balance factor of a node is calculated as the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. An AVL tree requires that the balance factor of every node stays within {-1, 0, +1}.

If an insertion or deletion pushes any node balance factor to plus two or minus two, tree rotations restore balance in O(1) time per affected node, guaranteeing maximum height proportional to 1.44 log n.

## Types of Tree Rotations

Single rotations handle monotonic imbalances: Right Rotation fixes Left-Left imbalance, and Left Rotation fixes Right-Right imbalance.

Double rotations resolve zig-zag imbalances: Left-Right rotation applies a Left Rotation to the child followed by a Right Rotation to the root; Right-Left applies a Right Rotation to the child followed by a Left Rotation to the root.

[54] # B-Trees

A B-tree is a self-balancing search tree data structure designed for disk storage systems, databases, and filesystems where read and write operations occur in large blocks of pages rather than individual memory words.

## Multi-Way Node Branching and Invariants

Unlike binary trees where each node has at most two children, a B-tree of order m (or minimum degree t >= 2) allows nodes to contain multiple keys and child pointers:
1. Every node has at most m children (or 2t - 1 keys).
2. Every internal node (except the root) has at least ceil(m / 2) children (or t - 1 keys).
3. The root has at least 2 children if it is not a leaf.
4. A non-leaf node with k children contains exactly k - 1 sorted keys that act as partition separators for its child subtrees.
5. All leaf nodes appear at the exact same depth, maintaining strict balance.

## Disk Access Minimization

Because disk I/O operations are thousands of times slower than main memory accesses, B-tree nodes are sized to match the physical page or block size of the underlying storage hardware (typically 4 KB to 64 KB). Large branching factors (e.g., m = 1000) keep the tree height exceptionally shallow; a tree of height 3 can index billions of records.

[33] # Exponential Search

Exponential search finds a target value in an unbounded or sorted array by identifying a bounded range and then executing a standard binary search within that range. It is especially effective when searching arrays of unknown size or when the target element is near the beginning of the collection.

## Algorithmic Range Doubling

The algorithm begins by checking whether the target resides at index 0. If not, it initializes an index pointer to 1 and repeatedly doubles the index (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...) until the element at the current index is greater than or equal to the target or the upper bound of the array is exceeded. Once the bounding interval [index/2, min(index, n - 1)] is determined, binary search is called over that sub-array.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

The range-bounding phase executes in O(log i) steps, where i is the index position of the target element. The subsequent binary search across an interval of length at most i also takes O(log i) comparisons. Consequently, exponential search runs in O(log i) time and O(1) auxiliary space, which strictly outperforms standard binary search when i is much smaller than the total length n.

## Practical Applications

Exponential search is standard in streaming architectures, memory-mapped files, and unbounded data sources where length queries are costly or impossible. It bridges unbounded step-skipping with logarithmic divide-and-conquer precision.

[56] # Binary Search Tree and Inorder Traversal

A Binary Search Tree (BST) organizes hierarchical node data where every node contains a key, optional data, and pointers to left and right child nodes.

## The Inorder Traversal Invariant

Inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes by processing the left subtree, evaluating the current node, and subsequently traversing the right subtree.

Because all keys in the left child are strictly less than the root, and all keys in the right child are strictly greater, an inorder traversal of a binary search tree outputs elements in monotonically increasing sorted order. This makes BST traversal a natural mechanism for producing sorted output in O(n) linear time.

## Search and Balancing

Search starts at the root, moving to the left child if the target is smaller and to the right child if greater, terminating when found or reaching a null leaf.

Average time for lookup, insertion, and deletion is O(log n). If elements are inserted in ascending or descending sorted order without balancing, the tree degenerates into a linear chain with O(n) worst-case depth.

sentence: ## Advantage of Hoare partitioning
Hoare partitioning has two advantages over Lomuto partitioning in the retrieved evidence:
It executes **fewer swaps**.
It **copes better with identical keys**. [48]
cited_text:
[48] # QuickSort Algorithm

QuickSort is an efficient comparison-based divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It selects a pivot value and partitions all remaining elements into values strictly less than the pivot and values greater than or equal to it.

## Partitioning Approaches

Lomuto partitioning maintains a boundary pointer and scans from left to right, swapping smaller items into position. Hoare partitioning uses two pointers scanning inward from both ends, executing fewer swaps and coping better with identical keys.

Modern sorting implementations often adopt dual-pivot partitioning. By using two pivots P1 and P2, the input is partitioned into three segments, yielding fewer comparisons and enhanced CPU cache performance.

## Complexity Bounds

Average-case time complexity is O(n log n). However, if pivot selection consistently isolates extreme elements, recursion depth degenerates to n, producing a worst-case time of O(n^2).

Randomized pivot choice or the median-of-three heuristic protects against worst-case degradation on presorted data. QuickSort requires O(log n) auxiliary stack space and sorts in-place.

The two pointers technique uses two indices traversing a linear collection to evaluate conditions without quadratic nested loops.

sentence: # Binary search vs. binary search tree (BST) search
Both methods use comparisons against a middle or current element to decide which part of the data to search next.

[32] # Binary Search

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array. It compares the target with the middle element. Then it throws away half of the array.

## Algorithmic Steps

Set lo to 0 and hi to the last index of the array. Compute mid as lo plus half of hi minus lo. If the target matches the value at mid, the search succeeds. If the target is smaller, move hi to mid minus one. Otherwise, move lo to mid plus one. Repeat until the boundaries cross.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

Each comparison halves the remaining search range. The runtime is strictly logarithmic O(log n) in both worst and average cases. The iterative approach uses O(1) auxiliary space, making it optimal for random-access indexed arrays.

Beyond exact value lookups, binary search generalizes to monotonic predicate functions, such as finding the first element where condition P is true. Variants such as exponential search and interpolation search build directly on this partitioning invariant.

[7] # The 0/1 Knapsack Problem

The 0/1 knapsack problem seeks to maximize total value from a set of items subject to a weight constraint W, where each item can either be taken or left behind.

## Recurrence and Subproblems

Because greedy selection of highest value-to-weight ratio can fail on discrete items, dynamic programming stores optimal values for subproblems dp[i][w], representing the maximum value using a subset of the first i items with capacity w.

For an item with weight wt and value val, if wt exceeds w the item cannot be taken and dp[i][w] equals dp[i-1][w]. Otherwise, dp[i][w] equals the maximum between excluding the item or including it: max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w - wt] + val).

## Optimization and Complexity

The time complexity is O(N * W), which is pseudo-polynomial since it depends on the numerical value of W.

Space can be compressed to a 1D array of size W plus one by iterating backwards from capacity W down to wt, preventing the current item from being used multiple times in the same pass.

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array. It compares the target with the middle element. Then it throws away half of the array.

An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree that maintains logarithmic lookup depth under insertions and deletions.

The array is recursively divided at midpoint index until individual base cases containing one or zero elements remain. During the combine phase, two index pointers read from the respective sorted halves and write the smaller element into an auxiliary buffer.

QuickSort is an efficient comparison-based divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It selects a pivot value and partitions all remaining elements into values strictly less than the pivot and values greater than or equal to it.

## Partitioning Approaches

Lomuto partitioning maintains a boundary pointer and scans from left to right, swapping smaller items into position. Hoare partitioning uses two pointers scanning inward from both ends, executing fewer swaps and coping better with identical keys.

Modern sorting implementations often adopt dual-pivot partitioning. By using two pivots P1 and P2, the input is partitioned into three segments, yielding fewer comparisons and enhanced CPU cache performance.

Average-case time complexity is O(n log n). However, if pivot selection consistently isolates extreme elements, recursion depth degenerates to n, producing a worst-case time of O(n^2).

QuickSort is an efficient comparison-based divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It selects a pivot value and partitions all remaining elements into values strictly less than the pivot and values greater than or equal to it.

## Partitioning Approaches

Lomuto partitioning maintains a boundary pointer and scans from left to right, swapping smaller items into position. Hoare partitioning uses two pointers scanning inward from both ends, executing fewer swaps and coping better with identical keys.

[31] # Kosaraju Algorithm

Kosaraju algorithm is a linear-time graph algorithm that finds all Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) in a directed graph using two consecutive Depth-First Search passes and the transpose of the input graph.

## Two-Pass Traversal Strategy

The first pass executes a standard DFS over the original graph G. When a vertex finishes all recursive explorations, it is pushed onto a stack. Consequently, the vertex that finishes last in the entire DFS forest rests on top of the stack, representing a sink component in the DAG of SCCs.

## Transpose Graph Processing

The algorithm then constructs the transpose graph G^T by reversing the direction of every edge in G. Reversing edges leaves the internal connectivity of every individual SCC invariant, while inverting the directed reachability between different SCCs.

## Second Pass Component Extraction

In the second pass, vertices are popped one by one from the stack. If the popped vertex has not yet been visited in G^T, a second DFS is launched from that vertex within G^T. All vertices reached during this traversal form an independent strongly connected component.

## Complexity Bounds

Constructing the transpose graph takes O(V + E) time, and both DFS traversals run in O(V + E) time. Thus, Kosaraju algorithm operates in Theta(V + E) time and O(V + E) space.

The balance factor of a node is calculated as the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. An AVL tree requires that the balance factor of every node stays within {-1, 0, +1}.

A treap (tree + heap) is a randomized binary search tree that assigns a randomly generated numerical priority to each inserted key. [52] # Topological Sort

Topological sort is an ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u comes before vertex v in the ordering. If a graph contains any directed cycle, no topological sort is possible.

## Kahn Algorithm using In-Degrees

Kahn algorithm maintains the in-degree of every vertex. It initializes a queue containing all vertices with an in-degree of 0. In each step, a vertex u is dequeued and appended to the topological order list. For every directed neighbor v of u, the in-degree of v is decremented by 1. If v reaches in-degree 0, it is enqueued. If the final ordered list contains fewer than V vertices, the graph contains at least one cycle.

## Depth-First Search Post-Order Traversal

Alternatively, topological sort can be performed using DFS. During traversal, vertices are marked with three states (unvisited, visiting, visited). If a visiting node is encountered, a back-edge and cycle exist. As each DFS exploration completes, the vertex is pushed onto a stack. Reversing the finish times or popping from the stack yields a valid topological order.

## Complexity and Applications

Both Kahn algorithm and DFS-based topological sort run in optimal O(V + E) time and use O(V) auxiliary space. Topological sorting is foundational for build dependency resolution, task scheduling, course prerequisite verification, and finding critical paths in project networks.

Graph traversal systematically visits nodes and edges in a network without cycling indefinitely.

## Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Breadth-First Search uses a queue to visit vertices layer by layer in order of graph distance from the origin. Starting at a root node, all immediate neighbors are visited before proceeding to distance two neighbors.

Because BFS explores outward evenly, it computes the exact shortest path in unweighted graphs. Time complexity is O(V + E) with O(V) space for the queue and visited state.

## Depth-First Search (DFS)

Depth-First Search explores deeply along connected branches before backtracking. It operates using recursion or an explicit stack.

[19] # Bipartite Matching

Bipartite matching finds the maximum set of edges in a bipartite graph such that no two edges share a common vertex. A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be partitioned into two disjoint independent sets, U and V, such that every edge connects a vertex in U to a vertex in V.

## Alternating and Augmenting Paths

An edge is matched if it belongs to the current matching M, and free otherwise. An alternating path is a path whose edges are alternately in M and not in M. An augmenting path is an alternating path that begins and ends at distinct unmatched (free) vertices. By Berge lemma, a matching M is maximum if and only if the graph admits no augmenting path with respect to M.

## Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm

The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm finds a maximum cardinality bipartite matching in sub-quadratic time. In each phase, it uses Breadth-First Search (BFS) to find the shortest augmenting paths and then Depth-First Search (DFS) to find a maximal set of vertex-disjoint augmenting paths of that shortest length.

## Complexity Bounds

[24] # Dijkstra Shortest Path Algorithm

Dijkstra algorithm determines the shortest path from a starting source node to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights.

## Relaxation with Priority Queue

The algorithm maintains a distance array initialized to zero for the source node and infinity for all others. A priority queue or min-heap tracks discovered vertices by minimum cumulative distance.

In each step, the vertex with the lowest tentative distance is extracted. For each outgoing edge to neighbor v, relaxation checks if the path through current node u provides a shorter distance than the previously recorded distance to v. If so, distance to v is updated and the pair is pushed to the min-heap.

## Runtime Complexity and Constraints

Using a standard binary min-heap, Dijkstra runs in O((V + E) log V) time. The algorithm is greedy and assumes that once a vertex distance is finalized, no future path can reduce it.

Because negative weights can violate this monotonic non-decreasing path distance property, Dijkstra fails on graphs with negative edges. In such scenarios, the Bellman-Ford algorithm must be used instead.

[32] # Binary Search

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array. It compares the target with the middle element. Then it throws away half of the array.

## Algorithmic Steps

Set lo to 0 and hi to the last index of the array. Compute mid as lo plus half of hi minus lo. If the target matches the value at mid, the search succeeds. If the target is smaller, move hi to mid minus one. Otherwise, move lo to mid plus one. Repeat until the boundaries cross.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

Each comparison halves the remaining search range. The runtime is strictly logarithmic O(log n) in both worst and average cases. The iterative approach uses O(1) auxiliary space, making it optimal for random-access indexed arrays.

## Invariant and Predicate Search

Beyond exact value lookups, binary search generalizes to monotonic predicate functions, such as finding the first element where condition P is true. Variants such as exponential search and interpolation search build directly on this partitioning invariant.

[47] # Merge Sort Algorithm

Merge sort is a stable divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that splits an array into halves, sorts them recursively, and merges the sorted halves into a single ordered sequence.

## The Merge Step

The array is recursively divided at midpoint index until individual base cases containing one or zero elements remain. During the combine phase, two index pointers read from the respective sorted halves and write the smaller element into an auxiliary buffer.

When one half is exhausted, the remaining items from the other half are copied over. Because each element is compared and placed once per tree level, the merge operation runs in linear O(n) time.

## Stability and Space Complexity

Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity across best, worst, and average cases. Its tree depth is strictly logarithmic with n operations performed per level.

Unlike QuickSort, merge sort is stable, preserving the original relative order of equivalent items. Standard array implementations require O(n) auxiliary memory for combining, whereas linked-list implementations can execute without auxiliary memory allocations.

Merge sort is a stable divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that splits an array into halves, sorts them recursively, and merges the sorted halves into a single ordered sequence.

## The Merge Step

The array is recursively divided at midpoint index until individual base cases containing one or zero elements remain. During the combine phase, two index pointers read from the respective sorted halves and write the smaller element into an auxiliary buffer.

When one half is exhausted, the remaining items from the other half are copied over. Because each element is compared and placed once per tree level, the merge operation runs in linear O(n) time.

## Stability and Space Complexity

Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity across best, worst, and average cases. Its tree depth is strictly logarithmic with n operations performed per level.

Unlike QuickSort, merge sort is stable, preserving the original relative order of equivalent items. Standard array implementations require O(n) auxiliary memory for combining, whereas linked-list implementations can execute without auxiliary memory allocations.

[32] # Binary Search

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array. It compares the target with the middle element. Then it throws away half of the array.

## Algorithmic Steps

Set lo to 0 and hi to the last index of the array. Compute mid as lo plus half of hi minus lo. If the target matches the value at mid, the search succeeds. If the target is smaller, move hi to mid minus one. Otherwise, move lo to mid plus one. Repeat until the boundaries cross.

Each comparison halves the remaining search range. The runtime is strictly logarithmic O(log n) in both worst and average cases. The iterative approach uses O(1) auxiliary space, making it optimal for random-access indexed arrays.

Beyond exact value lookups, binary search generalizes to monotonic predicate functions, such as finding the first element where condition P is true. Variants such as exponential search and interpolation search build directly on this partitioning invariant.

[7] # The 0/1 Knapsack Problem

The 0/1 knapsack problem seeks to maximize total value from a set of items subject to a weight constraint W, where each item can either be taken or left behind.

## Recurrence and Subproblems

Because greedy selection of highest value-to-weight ratio can fail on discrete items, dynamic programming stores optimal values for subproblems dp[i][w], representing the maximum value using a subset of the first i items with capacity w.

For an item with weight wt and value val, if wt exceeds w the item cannot be taken and dp[i][w] equals dp[i-1][w]. Otherwise, dp[i][w] equals the maximum between excluding the item or including it: max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w - wt] + val).

## Optimization and Complexity

The time complexity is O(N * W), which is pseudo-polynomial since it depends on the numerical value of W.

Space can be compressed to a 1D array of size W plus one by iterating backwards from capacity W down to wt, preventing the current item from being used multiple times in the same pass.

[33] # Exponential Search

Exponential search finds a target value in an unbounded or sorted array by identifying a bounded range and then executing a standard binary search within that range. It is especially effective when searching arrays of unknown size or when the target element is near the beginning of the collection.

## Algorithmic Range Doubling

The algorithm begins by checking whether the target resides at index 0. If not, it initializes an index pointer to 1 and repeatedly doubles the index (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...) until the element at the current index is greater than or equal to the target or the upper bound of the array is exceeded. Once the bounding interval [index/2, min(index, n - 1)] is determined, binary search is called over that sub-array.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

The range-bounding phase executes in O(log i) steps, where i is the index position of the target element. The subsequent binary search across an interval of length at most i also takes O(log i) comparisons. Consequently, exponential search runs in O(log i) time and O(1) auxiliary space, which strictly outperforms standard binary search when i is much smaller than the total length n.

## Practical Applications

Exponential search is standard in streaming architectures, memory-mapped files, and unbounded data sources where length queries are costly or impossible. It bridges unbounded step-skipping with logarithmic divide-and-conquer precision.

[34] # Interpolation Search

Interpolation search is an advanced search algorithm for sorted, uniformly distributed numeric arrays. It estimates the likely position of the target element based on key values at the search interval bounds, mimicking how a human searches a telephone directory.

## Probe Formula and Interpolation

Instead of calculating the median index, interpolation search computes a probe position using the linear interpolation formula: pos = lo + ((target - arr[lo]) * (hi - lo)) / (arr[hi] - arr[lo]). If arr[pos] equals the target, the search terminates. If arr[pos] is less than the target, the search continues in the right sub-array [pos + 1, hi]; otherwise, it resumes in [lo, pos - 1].

## Complexity and Distribution Sensitivity

For uniformly distributed datasets, interpolation search achieves an average-case time complexity of O(log log n), requiring far fewer comparisons than standard binary search. However, if the data distribution is non-uniform or exponentially clustered, the probe formula degrades severely, leading to a worst-case time complexity of O(n).

## Preconditions and Memory Model

Interpolation search requires both strict sorted order and direct O(1) random memory access. It assumes key values can be subtracted and scaled linearly, making it unsuitable for arbitrary non-numeric comparable objects without custom projection functions.

[8] # Longest Common Subsequence and Memoization

The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) finds the longest subsequence present in both strings in relative order without requiring elements to be consecutive.

## What is Memoization in Dynamic Programming

Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up recursive algorithms by caching the results of expensive function calls. When an identical subproblem with the same parameters is encountered again, the memoized value is looked up in O(1) time rather than recalculating the entire subtree.

In LCS, a naive recursion branches exponentially to O(2^(n+m)) due to heavily overlapping subproblems. Memoizing results in a lookup table reduces the execution time to O(n * m), turning an intractable problem into a polynomial one.

## Tabular Construction and Recovery

In bottom-up dynamic programming, a 2D matrix dp of size (n+1) by (m+1) is filled iteratively. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. If they differ, dp[i][j] takes the maximum of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1].

The final length resides at dp[n][m]. The actual sequence can be reconstructed by backtracking through the matrix from the bottom-right corner following matching cell transitions.

[41] # Two Pointers Technique

The two pointers technique uses two indices traversing a linear collection to evaluate conditions without quadratic nested loops.

## Inward Converging Pointers

For sorted collections, opposing pointers begin at index zero and the tail index. To evaluate whether two elements sum to a target, we compute their sum. If the sum is smaller than the target, incrementing the left pointer increases the total. If the sum exceeds the target, decrementing the right pointer decreases it.

This inward convergence processes the entire sorted array in O(n) linear time with O(1) auxiliary space, replacing nested search iterations.

## Sliding Window and Fast-Slow Pointers

In the forward-moving variation, both pointers start at the front. The leading pointer extends a candidate window to satisfy a constraint, while the trailing pointer contracts the window to minimize length or maintain invariants. In linked lists, Floyd cycle-finding uses two pointers moving at different speeds to detect loops in linear time without additional memory.

[38] # Sliding Window Algorithm

The sliding window algorithm maintains an active subarray or substring range defined by two boundary pointers, dynamically expanding or contracting to satisfy target invariants.

## Window Types and Mechanisms

In fixed-size windows, the distance between the left and right boundary pointers remains constant, computing aggregations such as moving averages or maximum sum subarrays in linear O(n) time.

In variable-size windows, the right pointer advances to expand the window until a condition is met (such as target character frequencies), and the left pointer contracts the window to restore the invariant or minimize window size.

## Relation to Two Pointers

While both sliding window and two pointers operate on linear sequences, two pointers frequently uses inward converging boundaries on sorted arrays (e.g., meeting in the middle for two-sum), whereas sliding window typically maintains contiguous intervals with forward-moving boundaries on both sorted and unsorted sequences.

[18] # Graph Traversal: BFS and DFS

Graph traversal systematically visits nodes and edges in a network without cycling indefinitely.

## Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Breadth-First Search uses a queue to visit vertices layer by layer in order of graph distance from the origin. Starting at a root node, all immediate neighbors are visited before proceeding to distance two neighbors.

Because BFS explores outward evenly, it computes the exact shortest path in unweighted graphs. Time complexity is O(V + E) with O(V) space for the queue and visited state.

## Depth-First Search (DFS)

Depth-First Search explores deeply along connected branches before backtracking. It operates using recursion or an explicit stack.

DFS is suited for topological sorting, cycle detection, and finding strongly connected components. A cycle in a directed graph is detected if DFS encounters an edge pointing to an ancestor currently residing in the active recursion call stack.

[53] # AVL Trees and Balancing Rotations

An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree that maintains logarithmic lookup depth under insertions and deletions.

## Height Balance Factor

The balance factor of a node is calculated as the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. An AVL tree requires that the balance factor of every node stays within {-1, 0, +1}.

If an insertion or deletion pushes any node balance factor to plus two or minus two, tree rotations restore balance in O(1) time per affected node, guaranteeing maximum height proportional to 1.44 log n.

## Types of Tree Rotations

Single rotations handle monotonic imbalances: Right Rotation fixes Left-Left imbalance, and Left Rotation fixes Right-Right imbalance.

Double rotations resolve zig-zag imbalances: Left-Right rotation applies a Left Rotation to the child followed by a Right Rotation to the root; Right-Left applies a Right Rotation to the child followed by a Left Rotation to the root.

[7] # The 0/1 Knapsack Problem

The 0/1 knapsack problem seeks to maximize total value from a set of items subject to a weight constraint W, where each item can either be taken or left behind.

## Recurrence and Subproblems

Because greedy selection of highest value-to-weight ratio can fail on discrete items, dynamic programming stores optimal values for subproblems dp[i][w], representing the maximum value using a subset of the first i items with capacity w.

For an item with weight wt and value val, if wt exceeds w the item cannot be taken and dp[i][w] equals dp[i-1][w]. Otherwise, dp[i][w] equals the maximum between excluding the item or including it: max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w - wt] + val).

## Optimization and Complexity

The time complexity is O(N * W), which is pseudo-polynomial since it depends on the numerical value of W.

Space can be compressed to a 1D array of size W plus one by iterating backwards from capacity W down to wt, preventing the current item from being used multiple times in the same pass.

[8] # Longest Common Subsequence and Memoization

The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) finds the longest subsequence present in both strings in relative order without requiring elements to be consecutive.

## What is Memoization in Dynamic Programming

Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up recursive algorithms by caching the results of expensive function calls. When an identical subproblem with the same parameters is encountered again, the memoized value is looked up in O(1) time rather than recalculating the entire subtree.

In LCS, a naive recursion branches exponentially to O(2^(n+m)) due to heavily overlapping subproblems. Memoizing results in a lookup table reduces the execution time to O(n * m), turning an intractable problem into a polynomial one.

## Tabular Construction and Recovery

In bottom-up dynamic programming, a 2D matrix dp of size (n+1) by (m+1) is filled iteratively. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. If they differ, dp[i][j] takes the maximum of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1].

The final length resides at dp[n][m]. The actual sequence can be reconstructed by backtracking through the matrix from the bottom-right corner following matching cell transitions.

[53] # AVL Trees and Balancing Rotations

An AVL tree is a height-balanced binary search tree that maintains logarithmic lookup depth under insertions and deletions.

## Height Balance Factor

The balance factor of a node is calculated as the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. An AVL tree requires that the balance factor of every node stays within {-1, 0, +1}.

If an insertion or deletion pushes any node balance factor to plus two or minus two, tree rotations restore balance in O(1) time per affected node, guaranteeing maximum height proportional to 1.44 log n.

## Types of Tree Rotations

Single rotations handle monotonic imbalances: Right Rotation fixes Left-Left imbalance, and Left Rotation fixes Right-Right imbalance.

Double rotations resolve zig-zag imbalances: Left-Right rotation applies a Left Rotation to the child followed by a Right Rotation to the root; Right-Left applies a Right Rotation to the child followed by a Left Rotation to the root.

[56] # Binary Search Tree and Inorder Traversal

A Binary Search Tree (BST) organizes hierarchical node data where every node contains a key, optional data, and pointers to left and right child nodes.

## The Inorder Traversal Invariant

Inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes by processing the left subtree, evaluating the current node, and subsequently traversing the right subtree.

Because all keys in the left child are strictly less than the root, and all keys in the right child are strictly greater, an inorder traversal of a binary search tree outputs elements in monotonically increasing sorted order. This makes BST traversal a natural mechanism for producing sorted output in O(n) linear time.

## Search and Balancing

Search starts at the root, moving to the left child if the target is smaller and to the right child if greater, terminating when found or reaching a null leaf.

Average time for lookup, insertion, and deletion is O(log n). If elements are inserted in ascending or descending sorted order without balancing, the tree degenerates into a linear chain with O(n) worst-case depth.

[32] # Binary Search

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array. It compares the target with the middle element. Then it throws away half of the array.

## Algorithmic Steps

Set lo to 0 and hi to the last index of the array. Compute mid as lo plus half of hi minus lo. If the target matches the value at mid, the search succeeds. If the target is smaller, move hi to mid minus one. Otherwise, move lo to mid plus one. Repeat until the boundaries cross.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

Each comparison halves the remaining search range. The runtime is strictly logarithmic O(log n) in both worst and average cases. The iterative approach uses O(1) auxiliary space, making it optimal for random-access indexed arrays.

## Invariant and Predicate Search

Beyond exact value lookups, binary search generalizes to monotonic predicate functions, such as finding the first element where condition P is true. Variants such as exponential search and interpolation search build directly on this partitioning invariant.

[33] # Exponential Search

Exponential search finds a target value in an unbounded or sorted array by identifying a bounded range and then executing a standard binary search within that range. It is especially effective when searching arrays of unknown size or when the target element is near the beginning of the collection.

## Algorithmic Range Doubling

The algorithm begins by checking whether the target resides at index 0. If not, it initializes an index pointer to 1 and repeatedly doubles the index (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...) until the element at the current index is greater than or equal to the target or the upper bound of the array is exceeded. Once the bounding interval [index/2, min(index, n - 1)] is determined, binary search is called over that sub-array.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

The range-bounding phase executes in O(log i) steps, where i is the index position of the target element. The subsequent binary search across an interval of length at most i also takes O(log i) comparisons. Consequently, exponential search runs in O(log i) time and O(1) auxiliary space, which strictly outperforms standard binary search when i is much smaller than the total length n.

## Practical Applications

Exponential search is standard in streaming architectures, memory-mapped files, and unbounded data sources where length queries are costly or impossible. It bridges unbounded step-skipping with logarithmic divide-and-conquer precision.

The two pointers technique uses two indices traversing a linear collection to evaluate conditions without quadratic nested loops.

## Inward Converging Pointers

For sorted collections, opposing pointers begin at index zero and the tail index. To evaluate whether two elements sum to a target, we compute their sum. If the sum is smaller than the target, incrementing the left pointer increases the total. If the sum exceeds the target, decrementing the right pointer decreases it.

This inward convergence processes the entire sorted array in O(n) linear time with O(1) auxiliary space, replacing nested search iterations.

## Sliding Window and Fast-Slow Pointers

In the forward-moving variation, both pointers start at the front. The leading pointer extends a candidate window to satisfy a constraint, while the trailing pointer contracts the window to minimize length or maintain invariants. In linked lists, Floyd cycle-finding uses two pointers moving at different speeds to detect loops in linear time without additional memory.

[47] # Merge Sort Algorithm

Merge sort is a stable divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that splits an array into halves, sorts them recursively, and merges the sorted halves into a single ordered sequence.

## The Merge Step

The array is recursively divided at midpoint index until individual base cases containing one or zero elements remain. During the combine phase, two index pointers read from the respective sorted halves and write the smaller element into an auxiliary buffer.

When one half is exhausted, the remaining items from the other half are copied over. Because each element is compared and placed once per tree level, the merge operation runs in linear O(n) time.

## Stability and Space Complexity

Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity across best, worst, and average cases. Its tree depth is strictly logarithmic with n operations performed per level.

Unlike QuickSort, merge sort is stable, preserving the original relative order of equivalent items. Standard array implementations require O(n) auxiliary memory for combining, whereas linked-list implementations can execute without auxiliary memory allocations.

[41] # Two Pointers Technique

The two pointers technique uses two indices traversing a linear collection to evaluate conditions without quadratic nested loops.

## Inward Converging Pointers

For sorted collections, opposing pointers begin at index zero and the tail index. To evaluate whether two elements sum to a target, we compute their sum. [56] # Binary Search Tree and Inorder Traversal

A Binary Search Tree (BST) organizes hierarchical node data where every node contains a key, optional data, and pointers to left and right child nodes.

## The Inorder Traversal Invariant

Inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes by processing the left subtree, evaluating the current node, and subsequently traversing the right subtree.

Because all keys in the left child are strictly less than the root, and all keys in the right child are strictly greater, an inorder traversal of a binary search tree outputs elements in monotonically increasing sorted order. This makes BST traversal a natural mechanism for producing sorted output in O(n) linear time.

## Search and Balancing

Search starts at the root, moving to the left child if the target is smaller and to the right child if greater, terminating when found or reaching a null leaf.

Average time for lookup, insertion, and deletion is O(log n). If elements are inserted in ascending or descending sorted order without balancing, the tree degenerates into a linear chain with O(n) worst-case depth.

[21] # Graph Cycle Detection

Cycle detection determines whether a graph contains at least one simple closed walk of length three or greater. Cycle detection algorithms vary depending on whether the graph is undirected or directed.

## Undirected Graphs using DFS or Disjoint Sets

In an undirected graph, a Depth-First Search maintains a visited array and tracks the parent of the currently visited vertex. If an adjacent neighbor is already visited and is not the immediate parent node, a back-edge exists, confirming a cycle. Alternatively, a Disjoint Set Union structure processes edges sequentially: if both endpoints of an edge belong to the same set, that edge forms a cycle.

## Directed Graphs using Three-Color DFS

In a directed graph, an edge pointing to a visited vertex is not necessarily a cycle (it could be a cross-edge or forward edge). Cycle detection uses a three-state coloring scheme:
1. White: unvisited node.
2. Gray: node currently in the active DFS recursion stack.
3. Black: node whose entire exploration has concluded.

If a directed edge encounters a Gray node, a back-edge pointing to an active ancestor has been discovered, confirming a directed cycle.

## Complexity Bounds

Both undirected DFS and directed three-color DFS visit every vertex and edge a constant number of times, executing in linear O(V + E) time and using O(V) auxiliary memory for colors and the recursion stack.

[18] # Graph Traversal: BFS and DFS

Graph traversal systematically visits nodes and edges in a network without cycling indefinitely.

## Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Breadth-First Search uses a queue to visit vertices layer by layer in order of graph distance from the origin. Starting at a root node, all immediate neighbors are visited before proceeding to distance two neighbors.

Because BFS explores outward evenly, it computes the exact shortest path in unweighted graphs. Time complexity is O(V + E) with O(V) space for the queue and visited state.

## Depth-First Search (DFS)

Depth-First Search explores deeply along connected branches before backtracking. It operates using recursion or an explicit stack.

DFS is suited for topological sorting, cycle detection, and finding strongly connected components. A cycle in a directed graph is detected if DFS encounters an edge pointing to an ancestor currently residing in the active recursion call stack.

[52] # Topological Sort

Topological sort is an ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u comes before vertex v in the ordering. If a graph contains any directed cycle, no topological sort is possible.

## Kahn Algorithm using In-Degrees

Kahn algorithm maintains the in-degree of every vertex. It initializes a queue containing all vertices with an in-degree of 0. In each step, a vertex u is dequeued and appended to the topological order list. For every directed neighbor v of u, the in-degree of v is decremented by 1. If v reaches in-degree 0, it is enqueued. If the final ordered list contains fewer than V vertices, the graph contains at least one cycle.

[21] # Graph Cycle Detection

Cycle detection determines whether a graph contains at least one simple closed walk of length three or greater. Cycle detection algorithms vary depending on whether the graph is undirected or directed.

## Undirected Graphs using DFS or Disjoint Sets

In an undirected graph, a Depth-First Search maintains a visited array and tracks the parent of the currently visited vertex. If an adjacent neighbor is already visited and is not the immediate parent node, a back-edge exists, confirming a cycle. Alternatively, a Disjoint Set Union structure processes edges sequentially: if both endpoints of an edge belong to the same set, that edge forms a cycle.

## Directed Graphs using Three-Color DFS

In a directed graph, an edge pointing to a visited vertex is not necessarily a cycle (it could be a cross-edge or forward edge). Cycle detection uses a three-state coloring scheme:
1. White: unvisited node.
2. Gray: node currently in the active DFS recursion stack.
3. Black: node whose entire exploration has concluded.

If a directed edge encounters a Gray node, a back-edge pointing to an active ancestor has been discovered, confirming a directed cycle.

## Complexity Bounds

Both undirected DFS and directed three-color DFS visit every vertex and edge a constant number of times, executing in linear O(V + E) time and using O(V) auxiliary memory for colors and the recursion stack.

[47] # Merge Sort Algorithm

Merge sort is a stable divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that splits an array into halves, sorts them recursively, and merges the sorted halves into a single ordered sequence.

## The Merge Step

The array is recursively divided at midpoint index until individual base cases containing one or zero elements remain. During the combine phase, two index pointers read from the respective sorted halves and write the smaller element into an auxiliary buffer.

When one half is exhausted, the remaining items from the other half are copied over. Because each element is compared and placed once per tree level, the merge operation runs in linear O(n) time.

## Stability and Space Complexity

Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity across best, worst, and average cases. Its tree depth is strictly logarithmic with n operations performed per level.

Unlike QuickSort, merge sort is stable, preserving the original relative order of equivalent items. Standard array implementations require O(n) auxiliary memory for combining, whereas linked-list implementations can execute without auxiliary memory allocations.

[48] # QuickSort Algorithm

QuickSort is an efficient comparison-based divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It selects a pivot value and partitions all remaining elements into values strictly less than the pivot and values greater than or equal to it.

## Partitioning Approaches

Lomuto partitioning maintains a boundary pointer and scans from left to right, swapping smaller items into position. Hoare partitioning uses two pointers scanning inward from both ends, executing fewer swaps and coping better with identical keys.

Modern sorting implementations often adopt dual-pivot partitioning. By using two pivots P1 and P2, the input is partitioned into three segments, yielding fewer comparisons and enhanced CPU cache performance.

## Complexity Bounds

Average-case time complexity is O(n log n). However, if pivot selection consistently isolates extreme elements, recursion depth degenerates to n, producing a worst-case time of O(n^2).

Randomized pivot choice or the median-of-three heuristic protects against worst-case degradation on presorted data. QuickSort requires O(log n) auxiliary stack space and sorts in-place.

[31] # Kosaraju Algorithm

Kosaraju algorithm is a linear-time graph algorithm that finds all Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) in a directed graph using two consecutive Depth-First Search passes and the transpose of the input graph.

## Two-Pass Traversal Strategy

The first pass executes a standard DFS over the original graph G. When a vertex finishes all recursive explorations, it is pushed onto a stack. Consequently, the vertex that finishes last in the entire DFS forest rests on top of the stack, representing a sink component in the DAG of SCCs.

## Transpose Graph Processing

The algorithm then constructs the transpose graph G^T by reversing the direction of every edge in G. Reversing edges leaves the internal connectivity of every individual SCC invariant, while inverting the directed reachability between different SCCs.

## Second Pass Component Extraction

In the second pass, vertices are popped one by one from the stack. If the popped vertex has not yet been visited in G^T, a second DFS is launched from that vertex within G^T. All vertices reached during this traversal form an independent strongly connected component.

## Complexity Bounds

Constructing the transpose graph takes O(V + E) time, and both DFS traversals run in O(V + E) time. Thus, Kosaraju algorithm operates in Theta(V + E) time and O(V + E) space.

[56] # Binary Search Tree and Inorder Traversal

A Binary Search Tree (BST) organizes hierarchical node data where every node contains a key, optional data, and pointers to left and right child nodes.

## The Inorder Traversal Invariant

Inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes by processing the left subtree, evaluating the current node, and subsequently traversing the right subtree.

Because all keys in the left child are strictly less than the root, and all keys in the right child are strictly greater, an inorder traversal of a binary search tree outputs elements in monotonically increasing sorted order. This makes BST traversal a natural mechanism for producing sorted output in O(n) linear time.

## Search and Balancing

Search starts at the root, moving to the left child if the target is smaller and to the right child if greater, terminating when found or reaching a null leaf.

Average time for lookup, insertion, and deletion is O(log n). If elements are inserted in ascending or descending sorted order without balancing, the tree degenerates into a linear chain with O(n) worst-case depth.

[54] # B-Trees

A B-tree is a self-balancing search tree data structure designed for disk storage systems, databases, and filesystems where read and write operations occur in large blocks of pages rather than individual memory words.

## Multi-Way Node Branching and Invariants

Unlike binary trees where each node has at most two children, a B-tree of order m (or minimum degree t >= 2) allows nodes to contain multiple keys and child pointers:
1. Every node has at most m children (or 2t - 1 keys).
2. Every internal node (except the root) has at least ceil(m / 2) children (or t - 1 keys).
3. The root has at least 2 children if it is not a leaf.
4. A non-leaf node with k children contains exactly k - 1 sorted keys that act as partition separators for its child subtrees.
5. All leaf nodes appear at the exact same depth, maintaining strict balance.

## Disk Access Minimization

Because disk I/O operations are thousands of times slower than main memory accesses, B-tree nodes are sized to match the physical page or block size of the underlying storage hardware (typically 4 KB to 64 KB). Large branching factors (e.g., m = 1000) keep the tree height exceptionally shallow; a tree of height 3 can index billions of records.

[24] # Dijkstra Shortest Path Algorithm

Dijkstra algorithm determines the shortest path from a starting source node to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights.

## Relaxation with Priority Queue

The algorithm maintains a distance array initialized to zero for the source node and infinity for all others. A priority queue or min-heap tracks discovered vertices by minimum cumulative distance.

In each step, the vertex with the lowest tentative distance is extracted. For each outgoing edge to neighbor v, relaxation checks if the path through current node u provides a shorter distance than the previously recorded distance to v. If so, distance to v is updated and the pair is pushed to the min-heap.

## Runtime Complexity and Constraints

Using a standard binary min-heap, Dijkstra runs in O((V + E) log V) time. The algorithm is greedy and assumes that once a vertex distance is finalized, no future path can reduce it.

Because negative weights can violate this monotonic non-decreasing path distance property, Dijkstra fails on graphs with negative edges. In such scenarios, the Bellman-Ford algorithm must be used instead.

[8] # Longest Common Subsequence and Memoization

The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) finds the longest subsequence present in both strings in relative order without requiring elements to be consecutive.

## What is Memoization in Dynamic Programming

Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up recursive algorithms by caching the results of expensive function calls. When an identical subproblem with the same parameters is encountered again, the memoized value is looked up in O(1) time rather than recalculating the entire subtree.

In LCS, a naive recursion branches exponentially to O(2^(n+m)) due to heavily overlapping subproblems. Memoizing results in a lookup table reduces the execution time to O(n * m), turning an intractable problem into a polynomial one.

## Tabular Construction and Recovery

In bottom-up dynamic programming, a 2D matrix dp of size (n+1) by (m+1) is filled iteratively. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. If they differ, dp[i][j] takes the maximum of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1].

The final length resides at dp[n][m]. The actual sequence can be reconstructed by backtracking through the matrix from the bottom-right corner following matching cell transitions.

The Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) problem finds the length of the longest subsequence of a given sequence such that all elements of the subsequence are sorted in strictly increasing order.

## Quadratic Dynamic Programming

In the standard dynamic programming formulation, dp[i] represents the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i. Initially, dp[i] = 1 for all i. For each i from 1 to n - 1 and j from 0 to i - 1, if arr[j] < arr[i], dp[i] is updated to max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1). The answer is max(dp[i] for 0 <= i < n). This approach runs in O(n^2) time and requires O(n) space.

The algorithm can be accelerated to O(n log n) time using patience sorting and binary search. It maintains an array tails, where tails[len - 1] stores the smallest tail element of all increasing subsequences of length len discovered so far. For each element x in arr, binary search (bisect_left) identifies the insertion point idx in tails.

[32] # Binary Search

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array. It compares the target with the middle element. Then it throws away half of the array.

## Algorithmic Steps

Set lo to 0 and hi to the last index of the array. Compute mid as lo plus half of hi minus lo. If the target matches the value at mid, the search succeeds. If the target is smaller, move hi to mid minus one. Otherwise, move lo to mid plus one. Repeat until the boundaries cross.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

Each comparison halves the remaining search range. The runtime is strictly logarithmic O(log n) in both worst and average cases. The iterative approach uses O(1) auxiliary space, making it optimal for random-access indexed arrays.

## Invariant and Predicate Search

Beyond exact value lookups, binary search generalizes to monotonic predicate functions, such as finding the first element where condition P is true. Variants such as exponential search and interpolation search build directly on this partitioning invariant.

[33] # Exponential Search

Exponential search finds a target value in an unbounded or sorted array by identifying a bounded range and then executing a standard binary search within that range. It is especially effective when searching arrays of unknown size or when the target element is near the beginning of the collection.

## Algorithmic Range Doubling

The algorithm begins by checking whether the target resides at index 0. If not, it initializes an index pointer to 1 and repeatedly doubles the index (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...) until the element at the current index is greater than or equal to the target or the upper bound of the array is exceeded. Once the bounding interval [index/2, min(index, n - 1)] is determined, binary search is called over that sub-array.

## Time and Complexity Analysis

The range-bounding phase executes in O(log i) steps, where i is the index position of the target element. The subsequent binary search across an interval of length at most i also takes O(log i) comparisons. Consequently, exponential search runs in O(log i) time and O(1) auxiliary space, which strictly outperforms standard binary search when i is much smaller than the total length n.

## Practical Applications

Exponential search is standard in streaming architectures, memory-mapped files, and unbounded data sources where length queries are costly or impossible. It bridges unbounded step-skipping with logarithmic divide-and-conquer precision.

[34] # Interpolation Search

Interpolation search is an advanced search algorithm for sorted, uniformly distributed numeric arrays. It estimates the likely position of the target element based on key values at the search interval bounds, mimicking how a human searches a telephone directory.

## Probe Formula and Interpolation

Instead of calculating the median index, interpolation search computes a probe position using the linear interpolation formula: pos = lo + ((target - arr[lo]) * (hi - lo)) / (arr[hi] - arr[lo]). If arr[pos] equals the target, the search terminates. If arr[pos] is less than the target, the search continues in the right sub-array [pos + 1, hi]; otherwise, it resumes in [lo, pos - 1].

For uniformly distributed datasets, interpolation search achieves an average-case time complexity of O(log log n), requiring far fewer comparisons than standard binary search. However, if the data distribution is non-uniform or exponentially clustered, the probe formula degrades severely, leading to a worst-case time complexity of O(n).

## Preconditions and Memory Model

Interpolation search requires both strict sorted order and direct O(1) random memory access. It assumes key values can be subtracted and scaled linearly, making it unsuitable for arbitrary non-numeric comparable objects without custom projection functions.

In each iteration, ternary search evaluates the target function at two test points and discards one-third of the search interval. [45] # Heap Sort

Heap sort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm that organizes array elements into a binary heap data structure to achieve in-place sorting with optimal worst-case guarantees.

## Heap Construction and Sifting

The algorithm begins by converting an unsorted array of n elements into a max-heap. Using bottom-up heapification, sift-down operations are applied starting from the last non-leaf node (index n/2 - 1) down to the root. Building the initial max-heap runs in linear O(n) time due to converging geometric series of node heights.

## Extraction and Sorting Phase

Once the max-heap is formed, the maximum element resides at the root index 0. The algorithm swaps the root with the last element in the active heap, decreases the active heap size by one, and invokes sift-down on the new root to restore the max-heap property. Repeating this process n - 1 times leaves the entire array sorted in ascending order.

## Complexity and Stability

[8] # Longest Common Subsequence and Memoization

The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) finds the longest subsequence present in both strings in relative order without requiring elements to be consecutive.

## What is Memoization in Dynamic Programming

Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up recursive algorithms by caching the results of expensive function calls. When an identical subproblem with the same parameters is encountered again, the memoized value is looked up in O(1) time rather than recalculating the entire subtree.

In LCS, a naive recursion branches exponentially to O(2^(n+m)) due to heavily overlapping subproblems. Memoizing results in a lookup table reduces the execution time to O(n * m), turning an intractable problem into a polynomial one.

## Tabular Construction and Recovery

In bottom-up dynamic programming, a 2D matrix dp of size (n+1) by (m+1) is filled iteratively. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. If they differ, dp[i][j] takes the maximum of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1].

The final length resides at dp[n][m]. The actual sequence can be reconstructed by backtracking through the matrix from the bottom-right corner following matching cell transitions.

The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm performs linear string pattern matching by exploiting structural redundancies within the search pattern. When a character mismatch occurs, it uses precomputed prefix-suffix overlap information to skip redundant character comparisons in the main text.

[37] # Rabin-Karp Algorithm

The Rabin-Karp algorithm searches for substrings by computing and comparing numeric hash values over sliding windows of the input text, using a rolling hash function to maintain linear average performance.

## Rolling Polynomial Hash

For a pattern of length m, Rabin-Karp treats the string as a base-b number modulo a large prime p: H(S) = sum(S[i] * b^(m - 1 - i)) mod p. When moving the sliding window from index k to k + 1, the new hash is computed in O(1) arithmetic operations: subtract the leading character's term, multiply by the base b, add the new trailing character, and apply modulo p.

## Collision Resolution and Complexity

When the hash of the current text window matches the hash of the pattern, an explicit character-by-character comparison verifies whether an actual match occurred, eliminating false positives caused by hash collisions. In the average case, with an appropriately large prime modulus, the number of spurious hits is negligible, yielding an expected runtime of O(n + m).

## Worst Case and Applications

If the hash function causes collisions on every candidate window, the runtime degrades to O(n * m). Rabin-Karp is especially effective for multi-pattern search, such as detecting plagiarism or searching a dictionary of keywords in a single text pass.
